name: Falcon’s top half
intro: This is where the top half of Falcon crashed into the Moon on 3 August 1971. It had lifted Dave Scott and Jim Irwin off the Moon the day before, on live TV, and was crashed on purpose after they moved into their command module, Endeavour. Its crater has not been found. The see-through cabin hanging here shows how Falcon’s top half looked before it hit.

hotspots.title: Somewhere here
hotspots.text: Falcon’s cabin hit about 90 km west of where it took off. Its crater has never been identified.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: A skimming crash
hotspots.text: It came in only about 3.2 degrees above the horizon at 1.70 km per second, so it probably smeared along the ground.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: Live on TV
hotspots.text: The day before, the rover parked at Hadley filmed this cabin blasting off, steered by a TV controller in Houston.

source.label: Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Apollo 15 video library

photo.alt: A fuzzy colour TV picture of the lunar module standing on grey ground under a black sky.
photo.caption: Falcon seconds before its top half lifted off, seen by the rover’s TV camera.

hotspots.title: Three listeners
hotspots.text: The seismometers at the Apollo 12, 14 and 15 sites all recorded the crash, giving scientists a test signal of known size and place.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: The ride home
hotspots.text: Under the cabin sat one small rocket engine with about 15,000 newtons of push. It had no throttle, only on and off, and it had to work the first time to lift the crew off the Moon.

hotspots.title: Only the top half
hotspots.text: This is just the top half of the lander: about 2.8 meters tall and a little over 4 meters wide. The bottom half served as its launch pad and is still standing at the landing site.

hotspots.title: Standing room only
hotspots.text: Two astronauts lived in this cabin while they were on the Moon. It had 6.65 cubic meters of room inside and no seats: they flew it standing up.

funFact: Its liftoff from Hadley was the first one ever broadcast live on TV, filmed by the parked rover’s camera.
whyLeft: With the crew safely in Endeavour, the cabin had no way home, so it was used to make one more moonquake.
repurpose: Only fragments remain, if they can be found. They would show how a spacecraft breaks up in a fast, skimming crash.

source.label: Estimate; never located (NSSDCA: impact point from tracking only)
